item.title: China proposes measures against foreign entities' infringement of trade secrets
item.description: China's commerce ministry released on Monday draft regulations for protecting trade secrets, proposing measures against foreign entities whose actions endanger or pose a real threat to China's national sovereignty, security or development interests.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: China's commerce ministry released on Monday draft regulations for protecting trade secrets, proposing measures against foreign entities whose actions endanger or pose a real threat to China's national sovereignty, security or development interests. The measures include restricting or banning the entities from making new investment in China and from importing or exporting goods and technologies related to China, according to the draft. The ministry is seeking public feedback on the draft regulations until November 24, it said in a statement.

item.title: Trump says Brazil election looked 'rigged', defeated Bolsonaro's party recognizes Lula win
item.description: "I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. "It looked very bad to me."
item.dc:creator: Oliver Griffin, Eduardo Simões
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump said on Monday that leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's surprise win in [USN:L2N46B01X TEXT:"Brazil's presidential vote"] "looked like another rigged election," although the party of defeated right-winger Flavio Bolsonaro later acknowledged the result. The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat in [USN:L2N46B01X TEXT:"Sunday's presidential election"], saying he would seek the annulment of Lula's victory after the Supreme Court extended voting by two hours. Later on Monday, however, Bolsonaro's Liberal Party said it [USN:S0N46906S TEXT:"acknowledged the runoff result"] in a statement signed by the party's head Valdemar Costa Neto. "We recognize the presidential election results," Costa Neto said. "But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified." Bolsonaro, who has not commented publicly since his party's statement, said earlier on Monday he would comply with a federal police order to hand over his passports following a visit to his father, who is under house arrest, and denied he was planning to flee Brazil. Trump did not endorse Bolsonaro ahead of the vote, although Reuters has reported that officials from his State Department [USN:L1N4650X8 TEXT:"led a campaign"] to return the Bolsonaros to power. "I didn't take sides, but it looked like another rigged election," Trump told reporters, without providing any evidence. "It looked very bad to me." Bolsonaro lost to Lula by over 4 million votes, a clear result that it will be challenging for him to overturn. Fewer than 35,000 votes, or some 0.03% of the total, were cast in the extra two hours of voting ordered by the Supreme Court, according to an analysis of electoral records by Insper professor Pedro Burgos. "I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated," Trump said. "The extension given was very strange." Vice President Geraldo Alckmin later defended Brazil's electoral system, saying in a TV interview with Rede Vanguarda that Trump's remarks were "totally wrong" and "unfounded." Neither Trump nor Jair Bolsonaro accepted their election losses in 2020 and 2022, respectively. Brazil's former president was handed a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing to Lula. Analysts do not expect Flavio Bolsonaro to be able to build the same anti-democratic movement as his father in 2022. MARKETS ROILED BY LULA WIN World leaders have already widely congratulated Lula on his unprecedented fourth mandate, which was greeted with [USN:L2N46C051 TEXT:"dismay by investors"] who had been betting on a Bolsonaro win. Brazil's real fell 8.1% against the dollar in its biggest one-day drop since 2002, while the stock exchange marked its steepest one-day fall since 2020. "The initial selloff could moderate as election-related positions are unwound, but investors will demand convincing fiscal commitments before rebuilding exposure," said Pantheon Macroeconomics' chief Latin America economist Andres Abadia. Lula's victory defied polls, precedent and global anti-incumbent sentiment to put the brakes on a wave of right-wing election victories across Latin America. He trailed Bolsonaro in the first round, but managed to convince voters to come out for him in the runoff. Pollsters said a higher-than-expected turnout and an improved [USN:L6N46815Z TEXT:"social media campaign"] helped power Lula to victory. During the campaign, Lula pointed to his track record of cutting poverty and inequality while also highlighting record-low unemployment, illiteracy and deforestation, but his fourth term may prove challenging. He will face an [USN:L6N46B06R TEXT:"uphill battle"] for his agenda in a Congress [USN:L6N45R137 TEXT:"packed with Bolsonaro allies"] after a surge of conservative voters in the first round of the general election pushed the Brazilian legislature further to the right.

item.title: Acciones y moneda de Brasil se hunden; reelección de Lula termina con racha alcista
item.description: Las acciones brasileñas y el real se hundieron el lunes tras la inesperada reelección del presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, lo que provocó la disipación del optimismo inversor que había surgido tras el éxito de su rival de derecha en la primera vuelta electoral.
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Campos, Marcela Ayres, Karin Strohecker
item.content:encoded: Las acciones brasileñas y el real se hundieron el lunes tras la inesperada reelección del presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, lo que provocó la disipación del optimismo inversor que había surgido tras el éxito de su rival de derecha en la primera vuelta electoral. El real brasileño se depreció un 8,36% a 5,4066 unidades por dólar, tras registrar un descenso del 12% al inicio de la jornada, uno de los mayores movimientos registrados y llegando a cotizar por sobre las 5,60 unidades. Mientras, el referencial bursátil (.BVSP) se desplomó preliminarmente un 13,43% a 177.539,81 puntos, en su mayor baja porcentual diaria desde marzo de 2020 y luego de perder más de un 16% en la sesión. La oleada de ventas afectó también a los bonos soberanos brasileños en los mercados internacionales; los títulos a más largo plazo fueron los más perjudicados, con la deuda con vencimiento en 2056 cayendo alrededor de 2,5 centavos. La bolsa brasileña detuvo sus operaciones durante 30 minutos después de que el índice de referencia Bovespa (.BVSP) cayera un 10% respecto a su cierre anterior, lo que activó el mecanismo de interrupción automática del mercado, informó en un comunicado B3, el operador bursátil. Los "credit default swaps" (CDS) a cinco años de Brasil, un indicador del costo de asegurarse contra un impago soberano, subieron hasta los 151,67 puntos básicos, frente a los 120,21 puntos del cierre del viernes, según datos de S&P Global Market Intelligence. Ante el desplome de los mercados brasileños, el Tesoro nacional canceló las subastas programadas de bonos gubernamentales, tanto los vinculados a la inflación como los de tasa fija, previstas para el 27 y el 29 de octubre, respectivamente. El colapso supone un giro drástico respecto a la tendencia alcista este mes, cuando los mercados subieron ante la expectativa de un viraje hacia la derecha, después de que Flávio Bolsonaro, hijo del expresidente Jair Bolsonaro, obtuvo inesperadamente el primer lugar en la primera vuelta de las elecciones presidenciales. El viernes, el índice Bovespa cerró casi un 7% por encima de su nivel previo a la primera vuelta, mientras que el real se había fortalecido cerca de un 5% frente al dólar. Los futuros de las tasas de interés también reflejaban la expectativa de que una política fiscal más restrictiva, bajo un eventual gobierno de Flávio Bolsonaro, permitiría una reducción en los costos de endeudamiento. La negativa del senador Bolsonaro a reconocer su derrota y su promesa de buscar la anulación de los resultados han aumentado la incertidumbre entre los inversores. "Un factor clave para los mercados financieros locales será la rapidez con la que Bolsonaro acepte el resultado, o al menos permita que el proceso constitucional siga su curso", afirmó Chris Turner, estratega de ING en Londres. Ahora, la atención se centrará en la elección de Lula para el cargo de ministro de Hacienda y en lo que esto revele sobre su enfoque fiscal. "La señal fundamental para los mercados será el compromiso de la futura administración de Lula con la disciplina fiscal, empezando por el nombramiento de un nuevo ministro de Hacienda en las próximas semanas", indicó Graham Stock, de RBC BlueBay Asset Management. DESAFÍOS Lula se enfrenta al reto de frenar el aumento de la deuda de Brasil, al tiempo que protege los programas sociales y la inversión. Los inversores buscan indicios de que su enfoque fiscal gradualista pueda reducir los costos de endeudamiento. "La administración de Lula no tendrá más remedio que llevar a cabo cierta consolidación fiscal, pero la mayoría de los inversores duda de que sea suficiente para encarrilar de nuevo la sostenibilidad de la deuda", comentó Thierry Larose, gestor de carteras en Vontobel Asset Management. Si no existe la confianza de que Lula pueda cumplir sus objetivos, los prestamistas podrían exigir tipos de interés más elevados, lo que aumentaría la carga de la deuda brasileña y encarecería el crédito para empresas y hogares. "Los inversionistas quieren un compromiso claro y creíble con la disciplina fiscal", dijo Alejo Czerwonko, director de inversiones para mercados emergentes de UBS Global Wealth Management. "Prevemos que el repunte que siguió a la primera vuelta ya esté en gran medida descontado en los precios, y que el ánimo se mantenga débil hasta que surja un plan fiscal claro". Czerwonko señaló que los inversionistas esperan que se ponga fin al gasto que acompañó a la campaña y que se trace una vía creíble para estabilizar la deuda pública. "Esto también implica una relación de trabajo con un Congreso de tendencia opositora, ya que ningún plan fiscal se aprueba sin él", añadió. El equipo de Lula se propone alcanzar un superávit presupuestario primario de alrededor del 1,3% del producto interno bruto para 2030. Eso dejaría fondos para cubrir parte de los intereses, reduciendo la necesidad de nuevos préstamos. Sin embargo, la deuda pública ya supera el 82% del PIB, mientras que las pensiones y otros gastos obligatorios por ley limitan las fuentes de ahorro. "Las políticas de Lula han hablado de recortes de gasto, pero no ha entrado en detalles sobre cómo se concretarán", señaló Divya Singaravelu, directora de investigación de Meridian 1305 Capital.

item.title: Brazil stocks, real tumble as Lula win shifts investor focus
item.description: Brazilian stocks and the real currency posted their sharpest losses in years on Monday after the surprise reelection of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva reversed recent market bets on a right-wing ascent to power.
item.dc:creator: Rodrigo Campos, Marcela Ayres, Karin Strohecker
item.content:encoded: Brazilian stocks and the real currency posted their sharpest losses in years on Monday after the surprise [USN:L6N4681ER TEXT:"reelection"] of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva reversed recent market bets on a right-wing ascent to power. Brazil's real , tumbled over 11% against the US dollar in early spot trading, one of its biggest intraday declines on record, while the benchmark Bovespa stock index (.BVSP) closed down 13.9% in its largest daily percentage drop since March 2020. The selloff also hit [USN:L5N46C0GQ TEXT:"sovereign debt"], with longer-dated bonds hit hardest and the 2054 maturity down 2.2 cents to yield 7.45% as Brazil's fiscal path came into focus. "Lula’s victory triggered a sharp market selloff as investors reassessed the fiscal outlook under his fourth term,” Mauricio Monge, senior Latin America economist at Oxford Economics, said in a report. His biggest challenge, Monge wrote, "will be to convince markets that he can deliver a credible, sustainable fiscal adjustment while prioritizing real wage growth and employment." TRADING HALTED Trading on Brazil's stock exchange was halted for 30 minutes after the Bovespa index fell 10% from its last close, triggering the market's circuit breaker mechanism, stock exchange operator B3 said in a statement. Earlier, B3 expanded the daily trading limits for Bovespa stock index futures, dollar futures and interest rate futures in response to heightened volatility. Brazil's five-year credit default swaps, a measure of the cost of insuring against sovereign default, jumped to 144 basis points from Friday's close of 120 bps, S&P Global Market Intelligence data showed. As markets tumbled, the Brazilian Treasury cancelled its regular auctions of inflation-linked and fixed-rate government bonds scheduled for October 27 and October 29, respectively. The real was down 8.1% to the dollar at 5.415 per greenback for its largest daily drop since at least 2002. Prices of raw sugar, of which Brazil is a major exporter, slid 5.6% on the collapsing exchange rate. The plunge is a sharp reversal from the rally earlier this month, when markets soared on expectations of a shift to the right after Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, unexpectedly finished first in the opening round of Brazil's presidential elections. The Bovespa closed on Friday almost 7% above its level before the first-round vote, while the real currency had been nearly 5% stronger against the US dollar over that period. Interest rate futures had also reflected expectations that tighter fiscal policy under a Bolsonaro government would make room for lower borrowing costs. Senator Bolsonaro's refusal to concede and his pledge to seek an annulment added to investor uncertainty. "Important for local financial markets will be how quickly Bolsonaro accepts the result, or at least allows the constitution to run its course," said Chris Turner, strategist at ING in London. CHALLENGES AHEAD Attention will now turn to Lula's choice of finance minister and what it signals about his fiscal approach. "The key signal for markets will be the next Lula administration's commitment to fiscal discipline, starting with the appointment of a new finance minister in coming weeks," said Graham Stock at RBC BlueBay Asset Management. Lula faces the [USN:L1N468127 TEXT:"challenge"] of slowing the rise in Brazil's debt while protecting social programmes and investment, with investors looking for signs his gradual fiscal approach can lower borrowing costs. "The more the fiscal pressures build, the more we see the debt burden rise without any clear, credible fiscal plan to bring deficits down over the longer term, that would start to raise more and more potential pressures for a change in the (credit rating) outlook to negative," said William Foster, senior vice president for sovereign ratings at Moody's and its lead Brazil analyst. Moody's rates Brazil's external sovereign debt Ba1, one level below investment grade, with a stable outlook. Without confidence that Lula can deliver, lenders could demand higher interest rates, adding to Brazil's debt burden and making credit more expensive for businesses and households. "Investors want a clear and credible commitment to fiscal discipline," said Alejo Czerwonko, chief investment officer for emerging markets at UBS Global Wealth Management. "We expect the rally that followed the first round to be largely priced out, and sentiment to stay weak until a clear fiscal plan emerges," Czerwonko said, adding that investors wanted a believable path to stabilize public debt. The reelected president's team has said it aims to produce a budget surplus of about 1.3% of gross domestic product by 2030. "Lula's policies have talked about spending cuts," said Divya Singaravelu, head of research at Meridian 1305 Capital, "but he has not gone into the details of how that is going to look."

item.title: Jordan says its air force struck 'militant hideouts' in Syria after church attack
item.description: Jordan said on Monday its air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week's deadly church attack in the kingdom were linked to "terrorist groups" operating there.
item.dc:creator: Abdelhadi Ramahi, Yasmine Ghania, Muhammad Gebaly
item.content:encoded: Jordan said on Monday its air force struck what it described as militant hideouts in southern Syria after determining that the suspects behind last week's deadly church attack in the kingdom were linked to "terrorist groups" operating there. The armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus. Syria's government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas. Damascus informed Jordan of its "complete reservation" over the strikes without prior coordination, the foreign ministry said in a statement. Seven people, including three children and a woman, were killed and three others were wounded in the Jordanian strikes, the Syrian Civil Defence said in a preliminary report. It said emergency teams responded to four sites hit by the strikes in the countryside of Daraa and Sweida provinces. There was no immediate comment from Jordan on that account. Shortly after the strikes, Syria closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan on Tuesday, suspending passenger and commercial traffic in both directions, citing developments on the ground in Daraa province, the Syrian General Authority for Border Crossings and Customs said in a statement. Nassib is Jordan's only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria. Earlier on Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law after a shootout on Monday over the church violence that killed nine people. "God willing, they only represent themselves," said Jordan's Director of Public Security, Major-General Obeidallah al-Maaytah. Such violence is rare in Jordan, a relatively stable US ally in the Middle East. Friday's attack on the Christian minority prompted King Abdullah to order security forces to respond with an "iron fist". In a press conference, al-Maaytah and Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said the country would not tolerate extremist terrorism. "The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are no indications of any links between them and other cells," al-Faraya added. ATTACK TARGETED GREEK ORTHODOX FUNERAL Friday's assault during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hamoud, about 120 km (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman, also wounded at least 34 people. [USN:L6N46B02Q TEXT:"Witnesses"] said gunmen opened fire for several minutes. The suspects, who lived near Hamoud, will face justice, said the security officials. The three suspects were named in the press briefing. Reuters video footage showed a building pockmarked by the exchange of fire in the village of al-Judayyda, in Karak governorate. Jordan's Public Security Directorate said in a statement carried by state media that security forces located the suspects while they were hiding in an abandoned house. They refused to surrender and attacked security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after wounding them. No security personnel were injured, and security forces found a number of firearms and rounds of ammunition in the suspects' possession. There has been no claim of responsibility for the church attack. Jordan, a US partner in the fight against extremism, has foiled Islamist militant plots in the past. The security officials did not name any Islamist groups in the press conference.

item.title: Australia's Perfection Fresh to seek $8.4 million penalty over price fixing, regulator says
item.description: Perfection Fresh Pty, Australia's second-largest vegetable supplier, admitted to fixing prices of vegetables sold to ALDI and agreed with the competition regulator to jointly seek a A$12 million ($8.43 million) penalty in court, the regulator said on Monday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Perfection Fresh Pty, Australia's second-largest vegetable supplier, admitted to fixing prices of vegetables sold to ALDI and agreed with the competition regulator to jointly seek a A$12 million ($8.43 million) penalty in court, the regulator said on Monday. Here are some details: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said Perfection Fresh admitted to fixing prices of broccoli, cauliflower and iceberg lettuce supplied to ALDI in New South Wales on 11 occasions between 2019 and 2020 The proposed A$12 million penalty covers nine contraventions and one attempted contravention of Australia's competition laws, the ACCC added The Federal Court will decide at a later date whether the proposed penalty and other orders are appropriate, the regulator said in its statement Perfection Fresh said in an emailed response it has reached an agreement with the ACCC concerning price fixing and has taken steps to strengthen its leadership, governance and compliance systems The ACCC began proceedings in September 2025 against Perfection Fresh, three other suppliers and three individuals over alleged price fixing. The case against the other parties is ongoing. ($1 = 1.4241 Australian dollars)

item.title: Euro slips ahead of central bank meetings, real tumbles
item.description: The euro fell against the dollar on Monday ahead of a busy week of central bank meetings and with crude oil prices remaining elevated, while the Brazilian real tumbled following a surprise election victory by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
item.dc:creator: Chibuike Oguh
item.content:encoded: The euro fell against the dollar on Monday ahead of a busy week of central bank meetings and with crude oil prices remaining elevated, while the Brazilian real tumbled following a [USN:L2N46B01X TEXT:"surprise election victory"] by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. The euro was pressured last week as a selloff in French government bonds drove the country's debt risk premium to its [USN:L6N4680QK TEXT:"highest level"] since the 2011 sovereign debt crisis, reigniting concerns about renewed financial stress across the euro zone. However, French government bond (OAT) prices rose on Monday after [USN:L1N469154 TEXT:"Moody's spared France"] a credit rating downgrade last week, easing pressure on a government struggling to shore up strained finances. The euro was down 0.21% against the dollar at $1.1179 but up 0.31% at 176.04 versus the yen . "The fundamental issue with the euro hasn't changed and spreads have tightened," said Kit Juckes, chief global FX strategist at Societe Generale. "Euro is still vulnerable at this point because the growth outlook isn't good and energy prices are still elevated." [USN:L2N46B09G TEXT:"Brent crude futures eased"] but still held near six-month highs. Elevated oil prices weigh on import-dependent economies such as the euro zone. Brent fell 0.78% to settle at $115.81 per barrel. The dollar has been supported by resilient US economic indicators, notwithstanding headwinds including rising inflation. The US currency [USN:L6N4680UP TEXT:"came under selling pressure"] during a tech-led market selloff last week. Five major central banks will announce policy decisions later in the week. The US [USN:L6N46606V TEXT:"Federal Reserve"], the [USN:L6N45U0QU TEXT:"European Central Bank"] and the [USN:L3N46C02N TEXT:"Bank of Japan"] are all expected to hold rates steady despite inflation pressures. [USN:L4N4690C8 TEXT:"New Zealand"]'s and [USN:L6N46911N TEXT:"Canada"]'s central banks are expected to raise rates this week. The Japanese yen fell 0.43% to 157.46 per dollar. The dollar index , which measures the US currency against a basket of peers, was up 0.31% at 102. "The dollar is doing less well than expected and has some headwinds but US economic data has been pretty resilient," Juckes said. REAL TUMBLES [USN:L2N46B01X TEXT:"The Brazilian real"] fell sharply against the US dollar after Lula won a historic fourth term on Sunday against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who is also the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Bolsonaro led the election's first round but lost in the runoff by over 4 million votes, rattling Brazilian financial markets, which had bet on his victory. He has refused to concede defeat and promised to ask for the result to be annulled. "While the risk of a more prolonged contesting of the election results has a negative impact on market sentiment, more fundamentally we think a greater degree of fiscal premium should be reflected in BRL and other local assets, especially as substantial fiscal easing has taken place over recent weeks," said Goldman Sachs analysts led by Teresa Alves in an investor note. "In our prior benchmarking of potential USD/BRL levels under more negative fiscal outcomes, we established 5.40 as a level consistent with the fiscal premium embedded in September 2024 (before additional fiscal measures were announced in November) and 5.80 as a level consistent with a greater degree of fiscal premium, akin to December 2024." The real was down 8.5% at 5.4 per dollar.

item.title: Japanese companies compensate users as cyberattacks buffet economy
item.description: Japanese companies are moving to pay compensation to users following waves of cyberattacks that have disrupted internet services and raised concerns about economic stability.
item.dc:creator: Kentaro Okasaka, Sam Nussey
item.content:encoded: Japanese companies are moving to pay compensation to users following waves of cyberattacks that have disrupted internet services and raised concerns about economic stability. GMO Internet Group (9449.T) , a leading provider of online financial services, said customers would be compensated for losses stemming from unauthorised access following a cyberattack on its foreign exchange trading service, and all customers would receive 5,000 yen ($32) as a gesture of goodwill, CEO Masatoshi Kumagai said in a blog post on Sunday. "The internet itself is now starting to break down," said Kumagai, whose sprawling group includes internet infrastructure and cryptocurrency trading. Shares of GMO, which had a market value of $2.6 billion as of Friday's close, slumped almost 16% on Monday to a four-month low against a 0.2% rise in Tokyo's benchmark index (.TOPX) . Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the government planned to compile an emergency package of measures against cyberattacks by next week. The government said on Friday it would set up a team to [USN:L1N469098 TEXT:"simulate cyberattacks"] using AI to identify weaknesses in technology systems as organisations scrambled to curtail risks from flaws in the [USN:L6N467127 TEXT:"PHP programming language"] that underpins much of the internet. More broadly, Japanese companies are being roiled by attacks, with industry experts saying AI is helping automate tasks from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns, making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect. "The internet is increasingly being transformed into a tool that malicious actors use to threaten and rob people," said Kumagai. Government and company websites in Japan, Europe and elsewhere [USN:L6N46813V TEXT:"went offline"] last week after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language prompted millions of hacking attempts. CALL ON JAPAN TO STEP UP CYBERDEFENCE Kumagai has urged the Japanese government to apply defence measures in response to the cyberattack, after the introduction of a cyberdefence system this month. The system could involve steps such as attacking hostile servers to neutralise threats. "Now is the time for the public and private sectors to work together to protect Japan," wrote Kumagai. GMO said it received a demand for money from a party believed to be behind the attack, along with a threat to disclose company and customer information if it did not comply. In an update on Monday to his blog post, Kumagai said that the party had demanded $50 million in cryptocurrency. GMO said it would not comply with the demand and would respond to the incident in coordination with police and other authorities. It did not mention any connection to PHP flaws. The company, which will provide a free alternative service to its customers for six months, said it could not currently calculate the impact on earnings from the goodwill payments and compensation for losses. White-hat hackers working for the company had identified security issues but the depth and speed of the response were insufficient, Kumagai wrote. CUSTOMER DATA PROTECTION WEAKNESSES The scale of recent cyberattacks has exposed weaknesses in Japanese companies' ability to protect their wealth of customer data and raised the prospect of surging costs to beef up defences. "Companies already have standard security measures in place, so if they want to strengthen them further, there is a possibility that the additional cost burden could be quite substantial," said Shoichi Arisawa, an analyst at IwaiCosmo Securities. There have been 723 cybersecurity incidents in Japan in the year to October 20, according to data from TrendAI — a unit of cybersecurity company Trend Micro — exceeding the annual totals in 2025 and 2024. "Reports may reflect both the threats organizations face and greater visibility into incidents that would previously have gone undetected, been underinvestigated, or remained undisclosed," said Satoshi Nagano, president of cybersecurity firm ESET Japan. Park24 (4666.T) , which operates the Times car-sharing service, said on Friday it would make 3,000-yen payments to customers following a personal data breach last month. The company said it would no longer retain identity document images after completing registration verification and expects to book an extraordinary loss of 5.5 billion yen due to responses to the attack and compensation payments. ($1 = 156.8100 yen)

item.title: World stocks gain ahead of 'formidable' week for risk; oil prices fall
item.description: Global shares advanced on Monday, with investors focused on central bank meetings and a week of corporate earnings that will test confidence in the AI boom.
item.dc:creator: Chris Prentice, Amanda Cooper
item.content:encoded: Global shares advanced on Monday, with investors focused on central bank meetings and a week of corporate earnings that will test confidence in the AI boom. Oil prices retreated after Friday's strong gains, amid signs of easing hostilities in the Middle East. Still, prices remained near recent highs as persistent attacks on key producer Saudi Arabia kept traders wary. The Houthi group in Yemen said on Monday it had attacked Saudi Arabia's [USN:L2N46C045 TEXT:"East-West crude oil"] pumping stations and Riyadh airport. MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe (.MIWD00000PUS) rose 4.22 points, or 0.38%, to 1,123.19. On Wall Street, major indexes climbed on tech strength after Anthropic's [USN:L3N46C10M TEXT:"initial public offering"] filing. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (.DJI) rose 146.42 points, or 0.28%, to 52,361.58, the S&P 500 (.SPX) gained 53.09 points, or 0.7%, to 7,676.77 and the Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) gained 214.04 points, or 0.83%, to 26,169.38. Brazilian stocks posted historic losses. The country's stock exchange [USN:L6N46C031 TEXT:"halted trading"] via a circuit breaker safety mechanism on Monday after [USN:L6N4681ER TEXT:"President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's reelection"]. His opponent refused to concede. In Europe, stocks rebounded on corporate optimism. The STOXX 600 (.STOXX) closed up 0.77%, led by gains in British technology services provider Computacenter (CCC.L) and Danish biotech Genmab (GMAB.CO) . ALPHABET, MICROSOFT, AMAZON AMONG REPORTING COMPANIES Traders awaited multiple central bank meetings and earnings from AI hyperscalers. [USN:L6N46919T TEXT:"Earnings"] are in store from Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) , as one-third of S&P 500 companies report. "The combination is formidable: megacap earnings, AI funding concerns, global semiconductor results, five major central bank meetings and potentially market-moving inflation and growth data," said Chris Weston, Pepperstone's head of research. "The danger isn't simply that markets move sharply. It's that one catalyst changes the interpretation of the next, creating feedback loops across equities, rates, FX and volatility," Weston added. [USN:L4N4690C8 TEXT:"New Zealand's"] central bank is widely expected to raise rates on Wednesday. Markets assume the US [USN:L6N46606V TEXT:"Federal Reserve"] will stand pat, but they imply an 80% chance that it will hike rates in December. Much the same is priced in for the [USN:L4N4650KC TEXT:"Bank of Japan"] and the [USN:L6N45U0QU TEXT:"European Central Bank"]. , , A key reading on US core inflation should show cost pressures remained elevated at 3.1% in September, while the economy is forecast to have grown at a brisk 3.2% annualized pace thanks in part to spending on data centers. "The most important risk is that oil futures are above our forecasts, largely reflecting concerns about potential further conflict with Iran," analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a note. "The more extreme and long-lasting the energy shock becomes, the more Fed participants will worry that inflationary pressures could broaden." Emerging market stocks (.MSCIEF) fell 15.13 points, or 0.96%, to 1,562.91. MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) closed 0.15% lower at 1,505.49. TREASURIES AND CURRENCIES The Brazilian real plunged after the presidential election. The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes was flat at 4.988%. The yield on the benchmark German 10-year Bund rose. In currency markets, the Japanese yen slipped 0.43%, and the euro was down 0.25% . The dollar index , which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.34%. Sterling dipped 0.24% , with Britain's new finance minister [USN:L1N46206Z TEXT:"John Healey"] set to deliver his first budget on Wednesday amid rising global borrowing costs and high energy prices due to the US-Israeli war with Iran. Spot gold rose 0.46% to $4,013.79 an ounce, rebounding from the prior session's more than three-month low. US gold futures settled 0.8% higher at $4,038.40 per ounce. Saudi Arabia, which along with Turkey and Pakistan was set to hold talks with Iranian officials in Tehran, said it was important to open channels for negotiations. On Sunday, Qatari mediators traveled to Tehran to try to de-escalate regional tensions in coordination with the United States, an official briefed on the situation said. Brent crude futures finished down 0.78% at $115.81 per barrel, as US crude settled down 1.46% at $101.76.

item.title: Britain will not join Canada-led defence bank initiative
item.description: Britain will not join the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, in a setback to efforts to create the world's first global defence bank, according to a person familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Britain will not join the Canada-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, in a setback to [USN:L1N44P0RH TEXT:"efforts"] to create the world's first global defence bank, according to a person familiar with the matter. The two countries instead said on Sunday that they would develop a framework for cooperation between their respective defence-funding initiatives, establishing two distinct but complementary institutions to support each other on investment opportunities and strategic challenges. "We have been working closely to consider how the Multilateral Defence Mechanism (MDM) and Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) can best advance our shared objectives," the statement said. The two governments were unable to agree on key issues including the location of the headquarters of a joint institution, the level of joint procurement, lending to members, and the rules around new members, a second person said. The MDM will focus on accelerating defence investment, joint procurement through financing, and bringing together demand across NATO allies to reduce procurement costs, while the DSRB will complement it by supporting investment in defence industries and supply chains, focusing more on single sovereign lending, the person added. The DSRB, which will be based in Canada, has [USN:L1N44P0RH TEXT:"faced"] challenges securing support from larger European nations. Reuters was first to report in September last year that Britain had declined to join the project. There were hopes Britain would reconsider its position under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham and his team. Germany had previously declined to join. A spokesperson for the German finance ministry said Germany was an observer in the negotiations on DSRB's charter and is reviewing open questions. Britain and Canada said the MDM and DSRB will be designed to work in close partnership, so they can support each other on emerging industrial priorities, investment opportunities and strategic financing challenges. AIMING TO RAISE BILLIONS The DSRB has been aiming to raise around €100 billion ($112 billion) and use the money to lend at low cost to governments and contractors for defence projects. It will also offer guarantees for lenders financing smaller firms seen as riskier borrowers. So far Albania, Belgium, Greece, Latvia, Luxembourg, Romania, Turkey and Ukraine have pledged their support, along with Canada. Canadian Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said the group would meet in Luxembourg on November 30 to sign articles of agreement establishing the bank. "Membership (is) open to other allies and close partners who share the Bank's objective," he said in a statement. Reuters previously [USN:L1N44P0RH TEXT:"reported "]that potential members had not joined because of concerns including whether the DSRB can offer cheaper financing than highly rated national governments as well as the amount of capital countries would need to commit, the bank's governance, and overlaps with existing initiatives. Britain's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had recently described the DSRB as a "really interesting and innovative mechanism" and said that he did not see the proposed defence bank and MDM as being in competition. Britain previously declined to join, citing concerns over value for money. Reuters [USN:L1N44P0RH TEXT:"previously reported"] that Burnham discussed the DSRB alongside the MDM initiative with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in July and with Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden during an August visit to Kyiv. ($1 = 0.8925 euros)

item.title: Trump invokes 9/11 in urging Michigan voters to oppose Muslim Senate candidate El-Sayed
item.description: If Abdul El-Sayed wins, he would be the first Muslim elected to the Senate. Trump has sought to paint the Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan as an anti-American Muslim radical.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump at a Sunday campaign rally ratcheted up his push to link US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to Muslim extremists, comparing him to the 9/11 attackers while saying Democrats would let violent anti-American terrorists into the United States. "I'm here to keep a jihadist, Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator," the president told a receptive audience in Port Huron, which is in a Michigan area where 66% of the vote went to Trump in the 2024 presidential election. If El-Sayed wins, he would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. Trump has sought to paint him as an anti-American Muslim radical, and on Sunday he took the rhetoric to a new level, likening El-Sayed to the attackers who took over United Flight 93 during the September 11, 2001, attacks. Michigan has one of the nation's most competitive US Senate contests going into the November 3 midterm elections, with former US Representative Mike Rogers, a Republican, and El-Sayed vying for an open seat that will help to decide control of the chamber. The president on Sunday compared voting against El-Sayed to the actions of Michigan native Todd Beamer and others who fought back against the Flight 93 hijackers. "Twenty-five years later, Michigan needs to stand up and fight, just like Todd did, to stop a jihadist from walking into the Capitol," said Trump. If El-Sayed wins, "he would be the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he's allowed to go in the Senate," Trump said. El-Sayed has dismissed the accusations against him, and at a Sunday night event, he suggested that Trump's frequent emphasis of El-Sayed's name contains a measure of hypocrisy. "I get that the president of the United States takes personal offense to my first name," El-Sayed told an audience in Grand Rapids, Michigan. "He doesn’t mind as much when it’s a shared name from the Saudis who are funding his son-in-law’s private equity, doesn’t seem to mind as much when it’s the Qataris who are giving him a $400 million private jet." Affinity Partners, Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner's investment fund, has reportedly received billions from a Saudi Government entity . Qatar gifted Trump a [USN:L1N42P11O TEXT:"Boeing 747 jet"]. EL-SAYED SAYS QUESTIONING HIS LOYALTY IS 'SHAMEFUL' The mostly White crowd at Sunday's rally cheered Trump’s comments on El-Sayed. Some attendees yelled “traitor” and others yelled “deport,” although El-Sayed was born in Michigan. Terrance Camburn, a 52-year-old disabled Army veteran from Sandusky, Michigan, said he supported Trump’s criticism because of El-Sayed’s “political beliefs.” “I’ve been down to Dearborn and I’ve seen many of the things he agrees with,” Camburn said when asked about Trump’s 9/11 comments. Dearborn, Michigan, has the highest per-capita concentration of Muslims of any US city. As he left the venue after the rally, Rogers did not respond to Reuters' questions about Trump's invocation of 9/11. But earlier on Sunday, he said on NBC's "Meet the Press" that he did not agree with the notion that El-Sayed is a violent terrorist. "I've never called him a terrorist," Rogers told NBC. Rogers has alleged without evidence that El-Sayed has [USN:L6N4661FE TEXT:"ties to the Muslim Brotherhood"], one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist groups. El-Sayed has denied affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood, saying it is "shameful" for Rogers to question his allegiance to the United States. Rogers told "Meet the Press" that El-Sayed had not sufficiently responded to questions about the allegations. "He's a Democrat Socialist of America-aligned candidate who has these pretty radical support groups that don't like America," he said. Trump's speech in eastern Michigan on Sunday came a day after former President Barack Obama campaigned for Democrats in the state, underscoring its importance in next week's elections. At a [USN:L6N46B03V TEXT:"Saturday rally"] in Detroit, Obama framed the attacks by El-Sayed's opponents as an attempt to make him look "less American than they are." The former president compared them to his own experience as the target of [USN:KBN23O2P2 TEXT:"false claims"] that he was born in Kenya. "This stuff didn't work on me," Obama said. "Not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul." Democrats need to gain just a handful of seats each in the US Senate and House of Representatives to overturn Republicans' narrow 53-47 and 218-214 majorities.
